Synchronization is a crucial capability for teams of agents, whether they are biological organisms or robotic systems, enabling them to carry out collective activities. This study examines a game-theoretic model of strategic multi-task synchronization among regular robot networks. These networks consist of regular graphs and are tasked with two objectives: maximizing team utility through vertex covering and minimizing energy consumption via a corresponding tradeoff function. The teams are divided into two groups that operate independently, with each group selecting one of the two tasks. We analyze a perfect information game where groups alternately decide on tasks and initial positions, followed by limited random walks to complete their assigned objectives. Our findings reveal that a stepwise linear energy consumption function yields a dominant strategy for prioritizing vertex covering, whereas a concave function makes it a dominant strategy to select the less coverable task first. Additionally, we derive a threshold for the average utility per unit of energy consumption in the stepwise linear scenario above which the group's optimal strategy changes. These results offer practical guidance for designing multi-task synchronization strategies in robot networks with specific energy consumption characteristics. To support these conclusions, we present a novel proof technique relying on a specific vertex labeling method for regular graphs, which may also benefit related research in this area. Finally, the proposed method is validated using 3-D-symmetric regular graphs of orders 15 through 21.

Mathematical models of epidemic dynamics serve as a vital bridge between theoretical insights and practical interventions during active health crises. This review offers a comprehensive overview of current models used to tackle the novel SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. We begin by detailing the basic reproduction number, a key metric for assessing a pathogen's potential to spawn epidemics, and how it is calculated. We then examine various models designed to predict epidemic trajectories and optimize control measures, as well as those focused on deriving epidemiological metrics from observational data to guide responses. Additionally, we discuss models aiming to elucidate the virus's biological mechanisms. By categorizing these models based on their primary objectives, we clarify that no single formulation can simultaneously optimize all goals or provide complete insights into SARS-CoV-2 epidemiology, evolution, and optimal management. Future research directions are also outlined. We hope this work engages the broader community, reminding them that statistical analyses relying on "meta-models" to forecast epidemics and control strategies must consider underlying biological processes and associated metrics to ensure their recommendations are effective and justified. Furthermore, the scientific community should strive to develop new models that integrate multiple objectives, goals, and metrics to offer the most holistic understanding possible of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic and its evolution. Such efforts could potentially enhance the extension of pandemic control measures beyond the specific models currently in use. This review provides the necessary background on epidemiological models and their applications during the present SARS-CoV-2 crisis, which will undoubtedly continue to evolve in the coming months and years, particularly as the world adapts to coexisting with this novel pathogen.

We investigate the connection between the back-reaction of emitted radiation and the temporal evolution of non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes through the shade thermodynamics framework. By treating the collapse of a radiation cloud as a non-equilibrium process, we define a corresponding "shade" cloud, whose mass represents the AdS black hole's mass post-radiation emission. Within this framework, we analyze the non-equilibrium dynamics of the mass, temperature, and entropy, both individually and along the temperature contour, during the emission process. The results demonstrate that the non-equilibrium mass, entropy, and shade temperature converge to their thermodynamic equilibrium values as the AdS black hole continues to emit radiation. Furthermore, we establish several theorems regarding the time-dependent evolution of the AdS black hole's mass and non-equilibrium shade temperature within the shade thermodynamics context under radiation emission. These findings indicate that, similar to an AdS black hole formed via collapse, one driven by mass emission also exhibits oscillatory temporal evolution of its mass when initially perturbed from equilibrium. Consequently, a charged AdS black hole oscillates toward thermal equilibrium as it emits radiation, with its oscillation frequency increasing as the system moves further from equilibrium. Finally, we explore the non-equilibrium dynamics of a Reissner-Nordström AdS black hole within the shade thermodynamics framework, highlighting the limitations of this approach for such systems.

Neural point cloud models represent a significant advancement in end-to-end tactical perception, particularly for automated tactical decision support systems (ATDSS). These models enable an ATDSS to perceive the tactical environment through a LiDAR simulator (TPC) rather than engaging with real live-fire assets. Consequently, Neural point cloud models can offer pre-battle predictions of how real assets would react to an attacking force's maneuvers. Unlike TCP models, which rely on camera images, point clouds provide a coordinate-based representation of the tactical scene that includes essential details often absent in images, such as the precise locations of friendly and enemy units. Furthermore, they offer an omnidirectional view of the tactical geography. Despite these benefits, point clouds typically contain a high volume of sparse data, a sparsity that can be exacerbated by the range and density of the LiDAR sensor used. To address this challenge and enhance the efficiency of both training and inference, this paper introduces Transformation-Unique Smoothing (USG). A specialized technique designed to manage point cloud sparsity, USG compresses data by eliminating redundant points caused by noise and sensor resolution. We evaluate our approach using a state-of-the-art encoder-decoder framework, demonstrating its efficacy through comprehensive comparisons against current best practices for both sparse and dense point clouds. Our results indicate that USG maintains the predictive performance of point cloud models while significantly boosting data efficiency: it cuts memory usage by 2.7x to 3.3x during training and by 3x to 4x during inference. Additionally, the technique accelerates inference by 1.4x to 2x and extends the effective range of a given point cloud sensor by approximately 10%. We open-source our implementation under the name TPC-USG. The code is available at: https://github.com/ATGL-Project/ATGL-UsG.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across multiple clients in a heterogeneous federated learning setup. Unlike conventional methods, our proposed Random Walk (RW) approach requires only minimal memory per client to share data with the PS. Specifically, clients do not need to transmit raw data or perform local model updates; instead, they simply track a "stroll" of data features.
